cue: There is no colour, only light and dark, and movement leaves trails.
rows: Every shark studied so far has only one kind of colour-sensing cell, so sharks are probably colour blind. They can tell apart shades of brightness that differ by less than 2 percent. This view shows the world in shades of grey.

Sharks see between a twentieth and a sixth as much detail as you do. Fast hunters of open water, like the bigeye thresher, are at the sharp end, and bottom-dwelling night hunters, like the Port Jackson shark, are at the coarse end. This view uses the middle of that range.

Many sharks, such as the lemon shark, see most sharply along a band level with the horizon, which lets them scan the sea floor or the open water without moving their eyes. This view sharpens a band along the horizon.
Sharks follow a flickering light up to 16 to 31 flashes a second, a quarter to a half of your rate, so quick movement smears for them. This view leaves trails behind anything that moves.

A shark’s eyes sit on the sides of its head, and in a lemon shark the two fields overlap by only about 10 degrees in front. Hammerheads swing their heads from side to side as they swim. This view sweeps slowly from side to side, at a pace the app has chosen, and holds still while you turn the phone.

Sharks feel the faint electric fields around living animals through gel-filled pores on the snout, called the ampullae of Lorenzini. A young hammerhead turns toward a prey-like field from about 30 centimetres away.
No phone can sense an electric field. In the lower part of this view, where things are taken to be close, living movement shimmers to stand in for one, and that glow is the app’s own invention.
A hunting shark usually smells its prey first and follows the scent upstream, then turns to sight, the lateral line, the electric sense and touch as it closes in. The picture leaves smell out.
